## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why5: Both boxes hold my own words, the office answering what it can and the after-hours, peak and holiday ring-outs, and nothing is reworded yet.
screens.why7: My four rungs sit on one measure, how soon a missed call was called back, best to worst, starting with a working rung, so Keel can add the fifth below them and the belief can be confirmed or refuted; but my first box names answering calls, not calling back the ones that rang out, so the act and the measure the rungs grade don't quite match, and I never mark where good enough ends.
screens.instead: First box: 'Calling back booking calls that rang out after hours, at peak or on holidays, from the missed-call list on the phone system'; second box: 'Called back within the hour (good enough) / All called back that day / Some called back when there was time / Few were ever called back.'

screens.why1: Right after I said how my people handle missed calls today, it makes sense to check how well that calling-back actually goes before the solution step.
screens.why2: Called back within the hour, called back that day and rang out are how any reservation agent in a Munich central office talks about the missed-call list.
screens.why3: An agent who worked the shift knows whether the missed calls on their list got called back and when.
screens.why4: The rungs slide from when calls were called back (within the hour, that day) to how many (some, few), and 'when there was time' gives a reason rather than an outcome, so an agent who called all back the next morning has no clean rung.
screens.why5: The scale is my own about calling back missed booking calls, and nothing of Codyco or the AI leaks onto it.
screens.why7: It has a working first rung, shortfalls below it and a line under the first so the belief can go either way, but the ladder mixes timing with share, and the last rung 'Calls that rang out were simply lost' is the card's named off-measure example where 'None were called back' belongs.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift with a missed call. How did calling back the missed booking calls go? All called back within the hour / All called back the same day / About half were called back / Only a few were called back / None were called back -- plus 'Someone else did it that shift'; line under the first.

screens.why1: Right after I said how my agents handle missed calls today, it makes sense to check the five outcomes Keel built from my answer and where the line sits.
screens.why2: 'Called back within the hour', 'that day' and 'days later' are how a reservations office talks about its missed-call list, so every row reads at a glance.
screens.why3: Any agent who works the missed-call list knows how fast it got worked on their last shift.
screens.why4: The common true answer for a booking call, that it was never called back and the guest booked elsewhere, is missing; 'Called back only weeks later' is nonsense for a room enquiry; and 'Some called back when there was time' is a share and a reason, not a time, so it overlaps the rungs around it.
screens.why5: My last rung, 'Few were ever called back', became 'Called back days later' and 'Called back only weeks later', which drops what I actually meant: most of those calls are simply lost.
screens.why7: There is a working rung above a line under the first, so the belief can be supported and refuted, but the last rung is not today's way failing outright ('Never called back'), and rung 3 grades a share and a condition instead of a step on the time-to-callback measure.
screens.instead: Every missed call called back within the hour · All called back that day · Called back the next day · Called back days later · Never called back -- line under the first

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my questions belongs right before the study goes out, after the problem rows are checked, and it asks nothing I have already answered.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain to me as a founder: a voice, a 5-second sample, a 400-credit cost that is the same either way, and a link sent by text message.
screens.why3: I can decide this myself by listening to two 5-second samples and knowing how my reservation agents expect to be spoken to.
screens.why4: Two named voices with samples are distinct and Daphne is preselected, but nothing says whether either speaks German, which is the first thing I need to know for agents at German hotel groups.
screens.why5: The screen only picks the interviewer's voice, so none of my wording of the problem changes and nothing of Codyco's product reaches the agent.
screens.instead: Who should ask your reservation agents the questions, in German? Daphne (German, ▶ 5 s) is picked for you, or Saskia (German, ▶ 5 s); same 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: Choosing how agents answer belongs just before sending, but it follows right after 'Who should ask them your questions?' and partly asks the same thing again: Daphne or not.
screens.why2: Plain to me: Daphne is named and explained in the option itself, and 'read and tap' is clear on first reading.
screens.why3: I know my agents sit at a desk or in a central office with guests and phones around them, so I can judge that a quiet read-and-tap suits them better than talking to a video.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete: AI voice, text, or let the agent pick, each described in plain words, and nothing is missing.
screens.why5: It says 'reservation agents', my own word, and nothing of Codyco's product leaks into how they answer.
screens.instead: Fold this into screen 16 as one question: 'How should reservation agents get your questions? Daphne asks them aloud on video / They read and tap, quietly at the desk / Let them pick when they open the link'.

screens.why1: After choosing how agents answer, deciding who gets the link is the natural last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three ways to reach people are plain to a founder, though 'Contacts page' assumes I know Keel's own page names.
screens.why3: I know whether I have named reservation agents from our 7 hotel groups or would post in a hotel-industry group.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel search list and an open group link cover the ways I'd reach agents, distinct and complete.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is changed or leaked; it is a pure sending choice.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right under the title, and the tally '4 beliefs: 4 holding' beside it is the number that decides it, tied by the line that the verdict is the worst of all its cards.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows what was counted, the 7 people and the bar, but Importance prints '6 of 7 put it in their two' twice and Frequency stacks a median, an in-range count and a bar on one line, so I have to read them twice.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence, Frequency and Current solution read like my beliefs, but the Importance line pastes my whole circumstance sentence into 'five things that are hard when...', which is recognisable but not how I would say it.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what four holding beliefs mean for Codyco, for example that the missed-call problem is real and I should go on to whether a director will pay €3,000 for the pilot. 'What it measures' only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible throughout, but 'Holding up' on all four beliefs from 7 reservation agents is never flagged as a small sample, and the 5% and seven-figure claims in the statement sit above the verdict as if this study had tested them.
screens.instead: All four problem beliefs held among the 7 agents who answered (every one let a booking call ring out this week, most on 6 days of 7). That is a small group, and the 5% rate was not tested here. Next, see whether directors will pay for the pilot.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 6 of 7, so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 7 cells for me on a 0 to 7 axis, with the marker at 6 labelled as my at least 8 in 10, so what is counted, out of how many and where my bar sits are all plain at once.
screens.why_b3: My band and window are kept, but the belief drops 'at hotel groups in Germany' from my segment and says agents 'let' a call ring out, which makes my missed calls sound like the agent's fault when the calls simply rang out after hours, at peak or on a holiday.
screens.why_b4: It tells me the problem is common among these 7 and points me to the next two cards, How often and Whether it matters, which is the right next step for a prevalence result.
screens.why_b5: n is visible, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and the So line limits itself to 'these 7', so nothing claims more than the answers carry.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 reservation agents at hotel groups in Germany had a booking call ring out unanswered in the last 7 days, and the gate should ask 'did you have a booking call ring out unanswered?'

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 inside my range against a bar of 5 of 7, with the median of 6 days, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Days out of 7, one cell per person, 7 counted and the bar at 5 are plain, but the legend's 'what you said' next to 'at what you said' and a 0 tick the agents could never pick made me look twice.
screens.why_b3: It's my 5 to 7 out of 7 and my missed calls, but 'let a booking call ring out' makes it sound like the agent chose to ignore the phone; I'd say a booking call went unanswered or was missed, and the trailing 'the most recent time it happened' doesn't belong on a count question.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' sends me onward but doesn't say what an almost-every-shift miss means for pitching a pilot to a reservations director.
screens.why_b5: 7 answered and 7 counted stay visible, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps 6 of 7 from being sold as proof.
screens.instead: Reservation agents missed a booking call on 5 to 7 days out of 7: 6 of 7 did (median 6 days), so it happens on most shifts, not just holidays. A lean from 7 people; whether those calls cost bookings is the next card.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits beside 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by what number, though the '6 of 7 put it in their two' line is printed twice.
screens.why_b2: The caption says 7 people, each picked two, bars count picks (14), my row is marked as the problem I named, and the strip shows 6 for and 1 against with the marker at 5.
screens.why_b3: My belief and my own row are recognisably mine, but the list isn't quite what I checked: 'Answering guests' questions about their stay' is gone, and 'Answering group requests over the phone' sits beside my email row as a near-twin, so 'five things' isn't my five.
screens.why_b4: The So line explains top-two versus first, which is useful, but it never says what this means for Codyco, such as that missed booking calls beat rates and group requests for these agents so the pitch can lead with them.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the screen says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so it claims nothing beyond these seven.
screens.instead: Holding up: 6 of 7 agents put booking calls before they ring out in their top two, ahead of rates, booking changes and group requests, so lead the pitch with missed calls; 7 is a lean, so confirm it with more agents. Show the rivals I typed, not an email and a phone version of the same group-request row.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, '7 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7', so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts people per rung over 7. The line under 'Every missed call called back within the hour' and the marker at 5 of 7 on an all-for strip read at first look.
screens.why_b3: Current solution and my rung 'Every missed call called back within the hour' are mine, but the belief narrows my job to 'calling back missed booking calls', and the asked line says 'your last booking call' where I meant a shift with a missed call, so it is reworded but recognisable.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' is a generic pointer; it does not say what the gap means for me, such as guests not called back for hours likely booking elsewhere, which is the case for an AI answering live.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible as 7 answered and 7 counted, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than these seven.
screens.instead: Say: none of 7 got every missed call back within the hour, and 5 called back only when there was time, so those guests likely booked elsewhere; next, test whether answering every call live is what closes that.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Holding up' and repeats it in the answer line, 'Importance held, 6 of 7', with the bar of 5 of 7 beside it, so the verdict and the number that decides it sit together.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is Importance and the belief line is my own: five hard things on a shift, with answering booking calls before they ring out among the two they would most like made easier.
screens.why_b4: The screen shows Chiara's why and her two picks but never says what to do about it, such as that groups whose call center already covers after hours are a weaker segment for me or that the email and rates pain sits next door.
screens.why_b5: The 7 stays visible, the single dissenter is shown as 1 of 1 asked, and 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 is called 'holding up', not strong, so nothing is claimed beyond the people who answered.
screens.why_b6: Chiara's quote adds something I did not type: where a call center covers the phones after six, the agent's day is eaten by group emails that arrive without rates, which points at a segment boundary and a neighbouring pain.
screens.instead: Importance held, 6 of 7 (bar 5); the one who disagreed has a call center covering the phones after six and loses her day to group emails with no rates, so groups that already cover after hours may be the weakest fit; ask whether they still miss calls at peak before selling to them.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks whether I am the person the study is for, and I can see why they ask.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call centre are what we call our own Munich office, so I can answer at once.
screens.why3: I know where I work, so I can answer this straight from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate question, and leaving out an escape is right here.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment, a hotel group's central reservations or call centre in Germany, and nothing about a product reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options I can hold after hearing it once, though 'I'll read 2 options' is a little stiff for a yes-or-no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I work in a central reservations office, asking whether a booking call went unanswered this week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Ring out' and 'booking call' are our words, but 'did you let' makes it sound like I chose to ignore the phone, so I'd hesitate before admitting it.
screens.why3: In our office the calls sit in the ACD queue and drop there while I'm on another line, so I don't see which ones ring out myself; my supervisor's abandoned-call report does, and I'd half guess.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this gate.
screens.why5: The founder counted calls that don't get answered, but 'let' turns that into my fault, which drifts from what they meant.
screens.why6: Short, one question, then 'Yes or no': easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.why7: The gate is on the problem rather than the routine, so a No is possible and the belief can be refuted, but 'let' at the head is the blame form the card says to put with its subject first ('had a call ring out').
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call to you ring out with nobody picking up? Yes · No

screens.why1: I just said yes to having calls ring out this week, so asking on how many days follows directly.
screens.why2: I understand it at once, but in our office we talk about calls dropping or callers hanging up in the queue, not calls I 'let ring out', which sounds like I sat there and ignored the phone.
screens.why3: Our calls queue through the system, so I see callers waiting and hanging up on the board rather than a phone I personally let ring, and on a trade-fair Saturday I'd be guessing which days it happened to me rather than to the office.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 is complete and distinct, and 'I can't recall' is the right way out for someone who said yes but lost track.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but 'did you let' puts the missed call on me personally, where the situation is calls the office as a whole fails to answer at peak.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and 'Say a number from 1 to 7, or say you can't recall' is easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.why7: Every option counts days of the 7-day window, from 1 to 7 with no zero and no bands, the unit is said once, the event is one act on a given day, and the single 'I can't recall' escape sits apart, so whether this supports or refutes the belief depends only on where the founder's low falls.
screens.instead: On how many of the last 7 days did a booking caller hang up waiting in the queue? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 7 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After asking how often I let booking calls ring out, asking which part of a shift on the line I would most like made easier follows naturally.
screens.why2: Rate, group requests and changes to existing bookings are our everyday words in the reservations office, so I can answer at first reading.
screens.why3: Every one of these is something I did on my last shift, especially on a trade-fair Saturday, so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: The two group-request rows differ only by email or phone, so they read as one task split in two, and a group request on the phone is also a booking call I have to pick up before it rings out.
screens.why5: Picking up booking calls before they ring out is there as the founder meant it, and nothing about a product or tool reaches me.
screens.why6: Five options is a fair number to hear, but three of them start with 'answering' and two are almost the same, so heard once they blur together.
screens.why7: The own row is present, not first, the escape is right and both for and against can happen, but the email row is in another channel and sits beside its phone rewording as one difficulty with another row, which bends the rivals' rules.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift on the booking line. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Quoting the right rate while the guest waits · Answering booking calls before they ring out · Taking group requests over the phone · Handling changes to existing bookings · None of these

screens.why1: After asking how often I let booking calls ring out, it is obvious to ask what happened to those calls afterwards.
screens.why2: The words are mine, but 'Think of your last booking call' points me at one call I answered, then asks about calling back all the missed ones, so I have to read it twice to know which occasion I am judging.
screens.why3: I know how our call-backs went on my last shift, but one 'last booking call' is not a time I called back missed calls, so I would guess which stretch it means.
screens.why4: The most common true answer in our office is missing: many missed callers are never called back at all because they have already booked elsewhere, and 'Called back only weeks later' is nonsense for a hotel booking; 'Some called back when there was time' also mixes a share with a reason and overlaps the day and days rungs.
screens.why5: Nothing of anybody's product reaches me, and calling back missed booking calls is how my office talks about the job.
screens.why6: It says well as five short options and one escape, but 'Every missed call called back within the hour' is a mouthful heard once, and the one-call anchor against a many-calls question trips the ear.
screens.why7: There are working rungs above a sensible line, but the last rung is not today's way failing outright ('never called back' is missing, 'weeks later' sits in its place), and 'some called back when there was time' breaks the one measure with a share and a condition clause.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift on the booking line. How soon were the missed booking calls called back? — All within the hour · All the same day · Some the same day, the rest later · Most only the next day or later · Never called back; or say someone else did it.
